passage: Kavitha, sit. You think you're the only one who feels lost at that college? When I went to Madras for my M.A., I was the first in my family to finish school, let alone university. My father drove a bus in Salem. Everyone in my class knew words I'd never heard: office hours, viva, citation. They called professors by name and argued with them. I thought, these people belong here, and I've sneaked in. I had first-class marks, but I sat at the back and never spoke. Then a girl from Tirunelveli, also the first in her family, found me in the library and said, "Shalini, you also don't know what a viva is, no?" We laughed so hard. We learned the codes together. That friendship made me stay, Kavitha. Find your people.

qa.q: What did the girl from Tirunelveli ask Shalini in the library?
qa.a: "Shalini, you also don't know what a viva is, no?"

qa.q: Why did young Shalini sit at the back despite first-class marks?
qa.a: Not knowing the words and habits others took for granted made Shalini feel like an outsider who had sneaked in, even with good marks.

qa.q: What turning point helped Shalini stay?
qa.a: Meeting another first-generation student and learning the unfamiliar codes together, which showed the gap was knowledge, not ability.

qa.q: What might Kavitha feel hearing this story?
qa.a: Kavitha may feel less alone and more hopeful, seeing that a respected elder once felt the same and found a way through with friends.

grounding: An elder recalls feeling out of place as a first-generation student despite good marks, until a fellow first-generation student helped with the codes.

passage: Parul's scholarship covered fees, not extras, so when her Delhi classmates booked the orientation trip to the hills, she said she had "family things" and stayed in the hostel. She had topped her district in Rajasthan. Here, she didn't know what "LMS" meant, or that you could email a professor, or why everyone laughed at a joke about a novel she'd never heard of. Her parents, who had never been to college, asked on the phone whether she'd made friends. "Yes," she lied. On the empty weekend she found a notice: "First-generation students' circle, Room 12, Sunday." She almost didn't go. Harish, a third-year from a farming family in Bihar, was running it. "LMS is just the website for assignments," he said. "Nobody tells us. So we tell each other." She stayed two hours.

qa.q: Where did Parul find the notice about the circle?
qa.a: In the hostel, on the empty weekend: "First-generation students' circle, Room 12, Sunday."

qa.q: Why did Parul tell her parents she had made friends?
qa.a: She felt out of place and alone, but didn't want to worry parents who had never been to college, or admit she felt she didn't belong.

qa.q: Which choice by Parul began to change things?
qa.a: Going to the first-generation circle despite nearly staying away, where others explained the unwritten codes like LMS.

qa.q: How might Harish see Parul at her first circle meeting?
qa.a: Harish likely recognises his own first year in her, and sees a capable student who just hasn't been told the rules yet.

grounding: A first-generation student with little money feels out of place despite top marks, and finds belonging in a peer circle.

passage: In her first month at the college on College Street, Bidisha noticed everything that marked her out. Her classmates spoke up easily in seminars and chatted about summer internships their parents had arranged. Her father ran a small cycle-repair shop in Howrah; nobody at home knew what a seminar was. Her first-term marks were among the best in the class, but she still ate lunch alone and felt like a guest who had come to the wrong house. One evening her roommate Lakshmi, from a fishing family near Chennai, admitted to feeling the same. "I thought it was just me," Lakshmi said. They started a chat group for students who were the first in their families to reach college. Twelve people joined in the first week.

qa.q: How many people joined the chat group in the first week?
qa.a: Twelve people.

qa.q: Why did Bidisha feel like a guest in the wrong house despite good marks?
qa.a: The easy talk of seminars and arranged internships was unfamiliar at home, so she read her unease as not belonging, even though her marks said otherwise.

qa.q: What choice helped Bidisha and Lakshmi most?
qa.a: Admitting the feeling to each other and starting a group for first-generation students, turning private doubt into shared support.

qa.q: What might it be like for Lakshmi to hear Bidisha felt the same?
qa.a: Lakshmi probably felt relief, since what seemed a lonely weakness turned out to be common among students like them.

grounding: A first-generation student feels out of place despite top marks, and finds community with others like her.

passage:
"Nitin, you've been quiet since you came home. College okay?"
"Fine, Bhabhi." Nitin pushed the rice around the plate.
Hafsa sat down across the table. "Your brother says you topped the first test."
"I did. But in class they talk about moots and internships and 'chambers', and I don't know what half of it means. Everyone's father is a lawyer. They all know the rules."
"And you think that means you don't belong?"
"I think it means I'm faking it."
Hafsa was quiet for a moment. "When I started nursing college, I didn't know what a viva was. I thought it was a test you could fail for being poor." She laughed. "It's just words, Nitin. You're learning the words. You already have the marks."
"There's a first-generation students' group. I saw a poster."
"Then go on Friday. Take someone from your bench."

qa.q: What did Nitin top?
qa.a: Nitin topped the first test.

qa.q: Why does Nitin feel like a fake despite topping the test?
qa.a: Nitin feels out of place and insecure, because classmates use codes (moots, internships, chambers) their lawyer parents taught them, so Nitin reads not knowing the words as not belonging.

qa.q: What turning point does Hafsa offer, and what choice follows?
qa.a: Her story about not knowing what a viva was reframes the gap as unfamiliar words, not ability; Nitin then thinks about going to the first-generation group on Friday.

qa.q: Why might Hafsa share her own nursing-college story?
qa.a: Hafsa seems to want Nitin to see that the lost feeling is common and passes, and that she understands it from the inside.

grounding: A first-generation law student with top marks feels like a fake among classmates who know the codes, and family points to community.

passage: My first semester at the engineering college in Pune, I ate lunch alone most days. I'm Hrithik, the first in my family to study past Class 10; my father repairs pumps in Latur. I had good marks, but everything else was a foreign language: "office hours", "electives", emailing a professor. I assumed everyone could see I didn't belong. When I got an A in circuits, I thought the grader had been sloppy. Then Pankaj, a third-year from a small town near Solapur, sat down with his tray and said, "You're in my hostel wing, right? Nobody tells you what office hours are. I'll show you." He took me to a first-generation students' meet that Saturday. Twelve of us, all confused by the same things. The A, it turned out, was just an A.

qa.q: Where does Hrithik's father repair pumps?
qa.a: In Latur.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik think the grader had been sloppy?
qa.a: Feeling out of place made Hrithik distrust any sign of belonging, so even a good grade seemed like a mistake rather than proof of ability.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it help?
qa.a: Pankaj explaining office hours and taking Hrithik to the first-generation meet; finding twelve others confused by the same codes showed the problem was unfamiliarity, not ability 🙂

qa.q: What might it mean to Pankaj to help Hrithik?
qa.a: Coming from a small town himself, Pankaj probably remembers the same confusion and is glad to spare someone else a lonely first semester.

grounding: A first-generation engineering student doubts belonging despite good marks until a senior and a peer group show it is unfamiliar codes, not ability.
